object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer entity identified by an account number. Every account can have subscriptions to products.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product or service offered to customers. Products are identified by product code and can have multiple subscriptions across different accounts.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: A billing artefact that specifies what a customer pays and how often. A price plan entitles the customer to exactly one feature bundle and is identified by a plan code.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature bundle representing what the customer gets: the feature set, number of seats, API access, SSO access. Multiple price plans can point to the same bundle.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement that an account pays a specified amount on a billing cycle for a product. Identified by subscription ID. Each account has at most one active subscription per product.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of when a subscription's price plan changes. Includes the new price plan, effective date, and who requested the change. Change date can differ from effective date.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history... It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The current operational state of a subscription. Exactly one status per subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency of billing for a subscription. Either monthly or annual, exactly one per subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual... Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription becomes active. Mandatory for all subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: Start date... Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription terminates. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date unless they are cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: End date, sometimes... An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: ChangeDate
object_types.definition: The date a plan change is made or recorded.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date a plan change takes effect for billing purposes.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record... we write a plan change with an effective date... Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.definition: A six-digit sequential identifier for an account. Unique and never reused.

object_types.definition: An identifier for the person or system that requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: Multiple meanings of 'plan': The term 'plan' is used to refer to at least two distinct concepts: (1) PricePlan (a billing artefact specifying price and frequency), and (2) FeatureBundle (the feature set the customer receives). Tom and Priya also mention that the sales team uses 'plan' to refer to negotiated deals, adding a third interpretation. The document clarifies this terminologically but leaves the business logic unresolved -- are these genuinely separate entities or should they be unified?

source_references.excerpt: Priya: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often... Tom: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise... Tom: We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: Identification of FeatureBundle: While the transcript establishes that FeatureBundle names (Starter, Professional, Enterprise) are unique, Tom notes 'There's no code, which annoys me,' suggesting a preference for a machine-readable identifier separate from the natural language name. Should a FeatureBundle have an additional synthetic identifier?

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

ambiguities.description: Composite uniqueness constraint on Subscription: The rule 'one active subscription per account per product' is stated as a composite constraint but modeled as two separate binary fact types (Subscription belongs to Account, Subscription is for Product). Does the ORM model properly capture this composite uniqueness? Should these be a single ternary fact type?

source_references.excerpt: An account can have a subscription to each of them at once... No. The system blocks it... One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.

ambiguities.description: Status vs. Paused flag overlap: Priya states that 'Paused' is a separate boolean flag but 'behaves like a status', and when querying for active subscriptions the system returns paused ones too. This creates a logical inconsistency in how subscription state is captured. Should paused be part of the SubscriptionStatus value constraint, or remain a separate attribute?

source_references.excerpt: Tom: There's also paused. Priya: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... Tom: It behaves like a status... Priya: which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: Handling of plan changes at subscription creation: The model assumes a subscription carries a 'current plan' field and plan changes are recorded separately. However, does a subscription created with a specific price plan count as already having a plan change, or is the initial state separate from the change history?

source_references.excerpt: we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history... And a brand new subscription has none.

ambiguities.description: MRR derivation vs. storage: The transcript clearly states MRR is derived from the price plan and billing period, not stored. However, it is visible in reporting dashboards and consumed by revenue analysis. Is it appropriate to exclude MRR from the conceptual model entirely, or should it be captured as a derived computed attribute for documentation purposes?

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term cancellation refund policy: The transcript identifies a conflict between documented system behaviour (no refund, access runs to paid-through date) and actual business practice (four goodwill refunds were issued last quarter). The stakeholders explicitly park this as undecided (finance and legal to resolve). The model captures the system rule, but should it also capture the unwritten policy or note the policy gap more formally?

source_references.excerpt: Tom: Mid-term cancellation on annual plans... Priya: Nothing happens. They've paid for the year... Tom: That's not what the pricing page implies and it's not what sales tell people... Sam: From a revenue perspective I need to know whether to treat those as contra-revenue or as a refund liability... Facilitator: Then I'm parking it explicitly... What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Change date vs. effective date distinctness: The model assumes every PlanChange has both a ChangeDate (when made) and an EffectiveDate (when it takes effect). The example (change made on the 3rd, effective on the 1st of next month) implies these are separate. However, are both always populated, or can they be the same? Is ChangeDate always earlier than or equal to EffectiveDate?

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

ambiguities.description: Subscriber to FeatureBundle relationship: The model captures that PricePlan entitles FeatureBundle, but does not directly capture a relationship between Subscription and FeatureBundle. Is there an implicit relationship (Subscription is for a FeatureBundle, derived via PricePlan), or should this be explicit?

source_references.excerpt: Every price plan gives you exactly one feature bundle.

ambiguities.description: Product life cycle: The transcript mentions a fourth product in discovery (not yet priced), and that new FeatureBundles can exist before price plans are created (Enterprise existed for two months without a price plan). The model does not capture whether Products are tied to FeatureBundles or are independent. Can one Product have multiple FeatureBundles over time, or is the relationship fixed?

source_references.excerpt: There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is... we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy.

ambiguities.description: Requester identity model: The model captures RequesterIdentifier as a value type but does not specify whether this is a user ID, email, or free-text name. What is the data type and uniqueness constraint for a requester?
